A pista estava nos grãos: ela acompanhou os padrões de cor ao longo de gerações de cruzamentos controlados. Quando o Ds saía do lugar, um gene da cor do grão deixava de ser suprimido por ele. McClintock propôs que esses "elementos controladores" regulavam genes, o que desafiava a visão do genoma como um conjunto fixo de instruções. Ela descreveu a reação dos colegas como "perplexidade e, em alguns casos, hostilidade" e, a partir de 1953, deixou de publicar sobre o tema. O quadro mudou nos anos 1960, quando François Jacob e Jacques Monod descreveram a regulação do operon lac, conceito que ela tinha demonstrado com o Ac/Ds em 1951, e outros cientistas confirmaram os mecanismos que ela vira. O Nobel de Fisiologia ou Medicina de 1983 premiou a descoberta mais de 30 anos depois da primeira descrição; até 2025, ela continuava sendo a única mulher a receber esse prêmio sem dividi-lo. O historiador Nathaniel Comfort, porém, contesta a ideia de que ela tenha sido marginalizada pelos colegas e chama essa narrativa de "mito McClintock". Os transposons, com seus restos sem função, somam mais da metade do DNA humano.

fontes.trecho: In early 1948, she made the surprising discovery that both Dissociation and Activator could transpose, or change position, on the chromosome. She observed the effects of the transposition of Ac and Ds by the changing patterns of coloration in maize kernels over generations of controlled crosses [...] When Ds moves, the aleurone-color gene is released from the suppressing effect of the Ds [...] McClintock's discovery challenged the concept of the genome as a static set of instructions passed between generations. [...] she described the reception of her research as "puzzlement and, in some instances, hostility". [...] Based on the reactions of other scientists to her work, McClintock felt she risked alienating the scientific mainstream, and from 1953 was forced to stop publishing accounts of her research on controlling elements. [...] The importance of McClintock's contributions was revealed in the 1960s, when the work of French geneticists François Jacob and Jacques Monod described the genetic regulation of the lac operon, a concept she had demonstrated with Ac/Ds in 1951. [...] McClintock's research became well understood in the 1960s and 1970s, as other scientists confirmed the mechanisms of genetic change and protein expression that she had demonstrated in her maize research in the 1940s and 1950s. Awards and recognition for her contributions to the field followed, including the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded to her in 1983 for the discovery of genetic transposition; as of 2025, she remains the only woman who has received an unshared Nobel Prize in that category. [...] It was given to her by the Nobel Foundation for discovering "mobile genetic elements"; this was more than 30 years after she initially described the phenomenon of controlling elements. [...] Comfort's biography contests the claim that McClintock was marginalized by other scientists, which he calls the "McClintock Myth"

Together with non-functional relics of old transposons, they account for over half of total human DNA. Sometimes called "jumping genes", transposons have played a major role in sculpting the human genome.

gancho: Células do tumor de Henrietta Lacks, tiradas sem consentimento em 1951, se multiplicam até hoje em laboratórios. São tão vigorosas que contaminaram outras culturas, e um biólogo propôs que viraram uma nova espécie.
explicacao: Henrietta Lacks, afro-americana de 31 anos, foi internada no Hospital Johns Hopkins, nos EUA, e tratada de um câncer do colo do útero. Em 8 de fevereiro de 1951, sem que ela fosse avisada ou consentisse, uma amostra do tumor foi para o biólogo George Gey. Até então, células humanas em cultura sobreviviam poucos dias, mas aquelas continuaram se dividindo. Henrietta morreu em outubro do mesmo ano. A linhagem, batizada de HeLa, serviu por exemplo para testar a vacina de Jonas Salk contra a pólio. O vigor teve um efeito colateral: as células HeLa se adaptam bem às placas de cultura, invadem e superam outras linhagens, e estimativas indicam que de 10% a 20% das linhagens celulares estão contaminadas por elas. Além disso, têm de 76 a 80 cromossomos, um número que não é o humano. Por isso o biólogo evolutivo Leigh Van Valen as descreveu como uma nova espécie, Helacyton gartleri, proposta que outros especialistas não levaram a sério. A genética trouxe outro capítulo: em 2013, o genoma de uma linhagem HeLa foi publicado sem o conhecimento da família, que temia o que ele revelaria sobre filhos e netos de Henrietta. No mesmo ano, um acordo com o NIH deu à família algum controle sobre o acesso a esses dados.

fontes.trecho: It is the oldest human cell line and one of the most commonly used. [...] The cell line is derived from cervical cancer cells extracted from the tumorous mass of Henrietta Lacks,  a 31-year-old African-American woman at the time, without patient notification or consent; this had occurred on February 8, 1951. [...] Lacks died of cervical cancer on October 4, 1951. [...] Cell biologist George Otto Gey developed Lacks's cell line upon noticing that her adenocarcinoma cells were particularly easy to be kept alive and multiply. Previously, cells cultured from other human cells would survive for only a few days, but cells from Lacks's tumor behaved differently, living for a very long time. [...] HeLa cells were used by Jonas Salk to test the first polio vaccine in the 1950s. [...] HeLa cells are sometimes difficult to control, because they adapt to growth in tissue culture plates and invade and outcompete other cell lines. [...] It has been shown that a substantial fraction of in vitro cell lines are contaminated with HeLa cells; estimates range from 10% to 20%. [...] Roughly speaking, the HeLa karyotype contains 76–80 total chromosomes [...] HeLa cells were described by evolutionary biologist Leigh Van Valen as an example of the contemporary creation of a new species, dubbed Helacyton gartleri, owing to their ability to replicate indefinitely and their non-human number of chromosomes. [...] However, this proposal was not taken seriously by other prominent evolutionary biologists, nor by scientists in other disciplines. [...] The complete genome and transcriptome of the Kyoto strain of HeLa cells were sequenced and published on 11 March 2013, without the Lacks family's knowledge.

There were objections from the Lacks family about the genetic information that was available for public access. [...] what information they can obtain from her sequencing that will tell them about her children and grandchildren and going down the line." [...] In August 2013, an agreement was announced between the family and the NIH that gave the family some control over access to the cells' DNA sequence found in the two studies

gancho: Exames para um transplante de rim indicaram que Karen Keegan não era a mãe biológica de dois dos filhos que ela deu à luz. A explicação: ela era uma quimera, formada pela fusão de dois embriões.
explicacao: O caso foi descrito em 2002 no New England Journal of Medicine. Karen precisava de um rim, e a família fez a tipagem dos genes HLA, que pesam na compatibilidade de transplantes. O sangue dela mostrava uma versão herdada do pai e uma da mãe. Dos três filhos, um tinha o esperado, mas os outros dois traziam uma versão do avô materno que ela não parecia ter. A pista veio de outros tecidos: em amostras de pele, folículos de cabelo, tireoide, bexiga e mucosa da boca, apareceram também as versões que faltavam. A explicação mais razoável é que a mãe de Karen liberou dois óvulos ao mesmo tempo, cada um fecundado por um espermatozoide, e os dois embriões se fundiram logo no início. Ela é uma quimera tetragamética, formada a partir de quatro gametas, como dois gêmeos não idênticos num corpo só. Não se sabe por que a medula óssea, de onde vem o sangue, tinha só uma das linhagens. O caso teve um lado bom: com os quatro conjuntos de antígenos de transplante, ela podia receber o rim de qualquer um dos irmãos ou da mãe sem medo de rejeição. A maioria das quimeras humanas passa a vida sem saber que é uma.

fontes.trecho: A report by Yu, et. al. in the May 16, 2002 issue of The New England Journal of Medicine documents the discovery of a tetragametic woman; that is a woman derived from four different gametes, not just two. She came to the doctors' attention because she needed a kidney transplant. Tissue typing, which is done with blood cells, showed her to have inherited the "1" HLA region of her father (who was 1,2) and the "3" region of her mother (who was 3,4). [...] Of her three sons, One was 1,6 which was to be expected, but the other two were both 2,5. The 5 they got from their father, but where did the 2 come from? The first thought was that she could not have been their mother, but clearly she knew better. [...] DNA analysis of her skin cells, hair follicles, thyroid cells, bladder cells, and cells scraped from inside her mouth revealed not only 1 and 3 but also 2 and 4. It is not clear why her bone marrow was an exception - containing only 1,3 stem cells. [...] The most reasonable explanation is that Her mother had simultaneously ovulated two eggs [...] Soon thereafter the resulting early embryos fused into a single embryo. [...] The HLA region on chromosome 6 carries a set of genes that encode the major transplantation antigens; that is, the antigens that trigger graft rejection. [...] But because this woman has all four sets of transplantation antigens, she can accept a kidney from any one of her brothers as well as her mother (her father was dead) without fear of rejecting it.

Most human chimeras will go through life without realizing they are chimeras. [...] Another case was that of Karen Keegan, who was also suspected (initially) of not being her children's biological mother, after DNA tests on her adult sons for a kidney transplant she needed seemed to show that she was not their mother. [...] Put another way, the chimera is formed from the merging of two nonidentical twins.

gancho: O "assassino do Golden State", autor de 13 assassinatos na Califórnia entre 1974 e 1986, foi preso em 2018 graças a parentes distantes que tinham posto o próprio DNA num site de genealogia.
explicacao: Joseph James DeAngelo, ex-policial, também cometeu ao menos 51 estupros e pelo menos 120 invasões de casas. A investigação durou décadas: em 2001, o DNA mostrou que duas séries de crimes com apelidos diferentes eram obra da mesma pessoa, mas o autor seguia sem nome. A virada veio quando os investigadores enviaram o perfil genético do criminoso, tirado de um kit de exame de estupro guardado no condado de Ventura, ao site de genealogia GEDmatch. O site apontou de 10 a 20 pessoas que tinham os mesmos tetravós que ele. Com a genealogista Barbara Rae-Venter, a equipe montou cerca de 25 árvores genealógicas; a que levou a ele tinha aproximadamente mil pessoas. Usando idade, sexo e local de moradia, os investigadores foram descartando nomes até restar só DeAngelo. Em abril de 2018, colheram o DNA dele às escondidas, na maçaneta do carro e num lenço de papel jogado no lixo, e as amostras bateram com as dos crimes. A técnica, chamada genealogia genética forense, se popularizou depois do caso, mas também gerou críticas sobre o uso de dados pessoais. Um artigo publicado na Science em 2018 estimou que uma busca desse tipo, para uma pessoa de ascendência europeia, acharia um primo de terceiro grau ou parente mais próximo em 60% das vezes.

fontes.trecho: is an American serial killer, serial rapist, and former police officer known as the Golden State Killer [...] who committed thirteen murders and numerous rapes and burglaries across California between 1974 and 1986. DeAngelo's crimes began in Northern California, where he committed a minimum of 120 burglaries and one murder in the San Joaquin Valley, before moving to Sacramento County, where he committed at least 51 rapes [...] In 2001, DNA testing indicated that the "East Area Rapist" and the "Original Night Stalker" were the same person [...] Once they uploaded the killer's DNA profile from a Ventura County rape kit to the personal genomics website GEDmatch. The website identified 10 to 20 people who had the same great-great-great-grandparents as the Golden State Killer; a team of five investigators working with genealogist Barbara Rae-Venter used this list to construct a large family tree. [...] investigators built about 25 different family trees. The tree that eventually linked to [DeAngelo] alone contained approximately 1,000 people. Over the course of a few months, investigators used other clues like age, sex, and place of residence to rule out suspects populating these trees, eliminating suspects one by one until only DeAngelo remained." On April 18, 2018, a DNA sample was surreptitiously collected from the door handle of DeAngelo's car; another sample was later collected from a tissue found in DeAngelo's curbside garbage can. Both were matched to samples associated with Golden State Killer crimes. [...] On the afternoon of April 24, 2018, Sacramento County Sheriff's deputies arrested DeAngelo

This investigative, or forensic, genetic genealogy technique became popular after the arrest of the alleged Golden State Killer in 2018, but has received significant backlash [...] In 2018, a paper in Science Magazine estimated that a DNA genealogy search on anybody of European descent would result in a third cousin or closer match 60% of the time.

gancho: Para a maior parte da humanidade, digerir leite fica difícil depois da infância, como nos outros mamíferos. Quem segue digerindo carrega uma novidade genética recente, que surgiu mais de uma vez, em lugares diferentes.
explicacao: A lactose do leite é quebrada pela enzima lactase. Na maioria dos mamíferos, a atividade dessa enzima despenca depois do desmame, quando o leite sai da dieta. Entre os humanos, a maior parte das pessoas do mundo também perde essa capacidade e, adulta, tem algum grau de intolerância à lactose. A persistência da lactase surgiu em algumas populações como adaptação ao consumo de leite de outros animais. As variantes associadas a ela não ficam no gene da lactase, mas numa região vizinha, dentro de outro gene, que funciona como um intensificador da atividade dele. E variam conforme a região: uma é muito frequente no norte da Europa; outras aparecem sobretudo no leste e no norte da África e no Oriente Médio. É um caso de evolução convergente, com várias origens. Caçadores-coletores de antes da Revolução Neolítica eram, em sua imensa maioria, intolerantes, e as variantes mais antigas só chegaram a frequências relevantes nos últimos 10 mil anos. Em algumas populações do leste da África, a persistência foi de quase ausente a quase universal em só 3 mil anos, sinal de uma seleção muito forte, cujo motivo exato ainda não se conhece. Quem não tem essas variantes ainda pode tolerar queijo e iogurte, porque a fermentação já quebrou parte da lactose.

fontes.trecho: Lactase persistence or lactose tolerance is the continued activity of the lactase enzyme in adulthood, allowing the digestion of lactose in milk. In most mammals, the activity of the enzyme is dramatically reduced after weaning. In some human populations though, lactase persistence has recently evolved as an adaptation to the consumption of nonhuman milk and dairy products beyond infancy. Lactase persistence is very high among northern Europeans. Worldwide, most people are lactase non-persistent, and are affected by varying degrees of lactose intolerance as adults. [...] They are all located in a region of the gene MCM6 upstream of LCT. This region is considered as an enhancer region for the transcription of LCT. [...] The T/G*-13915 allele is found mostly in populations from East and North Africa and the Middle East. The allele G/C*-14010 was identified in East Africa. [...] these show that lactase persistence has multiple origins in different parts of the world (i.e. it is an example of convergent evolution). [...] Hunter-gatherer populations before the Neolithic Revolution were overwhelmingly lactose intolerant, as are modern hunter-gatherers. Genetic studies suggest that the oldest alleles associated with lactase persistence only reached appreciable levels in human populations in the last 10,000 years. [...] The evolutionary processes driving the rapid spread of lactase persistence in some populations are not known. Among some populations inhabiting East Africa, lactase persistence has gone from negligible to near-ubiquitous frequencies in just 3000 years, suggesting a very strong selective pressure. [...] Individuals may lack the alleles for lactase persistence, but still tolerate dairy products in which lactose is broken down by the fermentation process (e.g. cheese, yoghurt).

gancho: A "Eva mitocondrial", ancestral de todos nós pela linha materna, e o "Adão do cromossomo Y", pela paterna, muito provavelmente não foram um casal. Nem precisam ter vivido na mesma época.
explicacao: As mitocôndrias passam só de mãe para filhos, e o cromossomo Y só de pai para filho. Seguindo essas linhas para trás, todas as pessoas vivas convergem numa única mulher, e todos os homens vivos, num único homem. Como quem ocupa cada posto depende de quais famílias deixaram descendentes, os dois não precisam ter sido contemporâneos, e as estimativas já oscilaram muito. Um estudo de 2000 pôs o Adão cerca de 84 mil anos depois da Eva; um de março de 2013 concluiu o oposto, com a Eva uns 140 mil anos depois. A descoberta, em 2013, de uma linhagem de Y mais antiga, a A00, empurrou o Adão para trás: por estimativas de 2015, ele viveu há algo entre 200 mil e 300 mil anos, enquanto a separação ligada à Eva foi estimada, em 2013, em cerca de 155 mil anos. Outro equívoco comum é imaginar que a Eva era a única mulher do seu tempo. O DNA do núcleo indica que a população efetiva de humanos antigos nunca caiu abaixo de dezenas de milhares; outras mulheres da época podem ter descendentes hoje, só que não por uma linha exclusiva de mães. E o título nem é fixo: quando a linhagem de uma filha da Eva some, ele passa para uma descendente mais recente.

fontes.trecho: As of 2013, estimates on the age of this split ranged at around 155,000 years ago [...] As the identity of both matrilineal and patrilineal MRCAs is dependent on genealogical history (pedigree collapse), they need not have lived at the same time. [...] One common misconception surrounding Mitochondrial Eve is that since all women alive today descended in a direct unbroken female line from her, she must have been the only woman alive at the time. However, nuclear DNA studies indicate that the effective population size of ancient humans never dropped below tens of thousands. Other women living during Eve's time may have descendants alive today but not in a direct female line. [...] When the mitochondrial lineages of daughters of Mitochondrial Eve die out, then the title of "Mitochondrial Eve" shifts forward from the remaining daughter through her matrilineal descendants [...] Sometimes Mitochondrial Eve is assumed to have lived at the same time as Y-chromosomal Adam (from whom all living males are descended patrilineally), and perhaps even met and mated with him. Even if this were true, which is currently regarded as highly unlikely, this would only be a coincidence. [...] A recent study (March 2013) concluded however that "Eve" lived much later than "Adam" – some 140,000 years later.

Thomson et al. 2000, which proposed an age of about 59,000. This date suggested that the Y-MRCA lived about 84,000 years after his female counterpart mt-MRCA [...] As of 2018, this is haplogroup A00 (discovered in 2013). [...] the discovery of the archaic Y-haplogroup has pushed back the estimated age of the Y-MRCA beyond the most likely age of the mt-MRCA. As of 2015, estimates of the age of the Y-MRCA range around 200,000 to 300,000 years ago

gancho: O genoma humano foi declarado completo em 2003, mas faltavam cerca de 8%, um volume comparável a um cromossomo inteiro. A sequência sem lacunas só saiu em 2022, e o cromossomo Y só foi concluído em 2023.
explicacao: O Projeto Genoma Humano, de 3 bilhões de dólares, foi lançado oficialmente em 1990 e declarado concluído em 14 de abril de 2003. Mas o objetivo era sequenciar só as regiões de eucromatina, que somam 92,1% do genoma. Os 7,9% restantes ficam em regiões como os centrômeros e os telômeros, mais difíceis de ler e que ficaram fora dos planos originais. Nessas partes há muito DNA repetitivo, e as técnicas de leitura curta, que leem algumas centenas de letras por vez, deixavam buracos na montagem. O consórcio Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) resolveu isso combinando dois métodos de leitura longa: um lê até 1 milhão de letras de uma vez, com precisão modesta; o outro, cerca de 20 mil, quase sem erros. Também usou uma linhagem de células em que as duas cópias de cada cromossomo são idênticas, o que evita misturar as duas versões diferentes que a maioria das células humanas carrega. A sequência completa saiu em seis artigos na revista Science em 2022. Os 8% finais incluem vários genes, e a nova referência permitiu achar mais de 2 milhões de variantes genéticas adicionais. O cromossomo Y, muito repetitivo, só teve a sequência completa publicada em agosto de 2023.

fontes.titulo: Researchers generate the first complete, gapless sequence of a human genome (NHGRI, 2022)
fontes.trecho: Scientists have published the first complete, gapless sequence of a human genome, two decades after the Human Genome Project produced the first draft human genome sequence. [...] The T2T consortium used the now-complete genome sequence as a reference to discover more than 2 million additional variants in the human genome. [...] The full sequencing builds upon the work of the Human Genome Project, which mapped about 92% of the genome [...] Six papers encompassing the completed sequence appear in Science [...] That last 8% includes numerous genes and repetitive DNA and is comparable in size to an entire chromosome. [...] The cost of sequencing a human genome using “short-read” technologies, which provide several hundred bases of DNA sequence at a time, is only a few hundred dollars [...] However, using these short-read methods alone still leaves some gaps in assembled genome sequences. [...] The Oxford Nanopore DNA sequencing method can read up to 1 million DNA letters in a single read with modest accuracy, while the PacBio HiFi DNA sequencing method can read about 20,000 letters with nearly perfect accuracy. Researchers in the T2T consortium used both DNA sequencing methods to generate the complete human genome sequence.

It was declared complete on 14 April 2003, and included about 92% of the genome. [...] In April 2022, the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium published a complete sequence of the non-Y chromosomes, highlighting the 8% of the human genome that the HGP had not sequenced. [...] The full sequence of the Y chromosome was only published in August 2023 due to challenges with sequencing and assembling, caused by its highly repetitive nature. [...] the aim was to sequence only euchromatic regions of the nuclear genome, which make up 92.1% of the human genome. The remaining 7.9% exists in scattered heterochromatic regions such as those found in centromeres and telomeres. These regions by their nature are generally more difficult to sequence and so were not included as part of the project's original plans. [...] The $3 billion project was formally founded in 1990 [...] a hydatidiform mole-derived cell line in which both copies of each chromosome are identical

gancho: Um gene essencial para formar o cérebro, a medula espinhal e os dedos de um embrião se chama "sonic hedgehog", em homenagem ao Sonic do videogame. O nome divertido virou problema na hora de falar com pacientes.
explicacao: A história começa com o gene hedgehog ("ouriço") da mosca-das-frutas, identificado em estudos publicados em 1980 que renderam um Nobel em 1995. Sem esse gene, o embrião da mosca fica coberto de pequenas pontas, parecidas com os espinhos de um ouriço. Ao procurar equivalentes em vertebrados, pesquisadores acharam três genes. Dois ganharam nomes de espécies de ouriço: desert hedgehog e Indian hedgehog. O terceiro foi batizado por Robert Riddle, pós-doutorando no laboratório de Clifford Tabin, depois que a esposa dele chegou em casa com uma revista que trazia um anúncio do primeiro jogo do Sonic, de 1991. O gene produz um sinal cuja concentração varia ao longo do embrião e orienta o destino das células na formação de partes do cérebro, da medula espinhal, dos pulmões e dos dentes; o desenvolvimento dos membros e dos dedos depende dele. Mutações nesse gene podem causar holoprosencefalia, em que o cérebro anterior não se divide nos lados direito e esquerdo, com possíveis defeitos graves no crânio e no rosto. Por isso, alguns médicos e cientistas acharam o nome frívolo demais: falar de uma mutação no "sonic hedgehog" pode soar mal numa conversa sobre uma doença séria. A polêmica esfriou, e com pacientes e famílias se usam as siglas padronizadas.

fontes.trecho: Sonic hedgehog is a morphogen that patterns the developing embryo using a concentration gradient [...] Mutations in this gene can contribute to the development of holoprosencephaly, a developmental anomaly in which an embryo's forebrain fails to split the right and left sides of the brain. [...] The hedgehog gene (hh) was first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster in the classic Heidelberg screens of Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and Eric Wieschaus, as published in 1980. These screens, which led to the researchers winning a Nobel Prize in 1995 along with developmental geneticist Edward B. Lewis [...] The hh loss of function mutant phenotype causes the embryos to be covered with denticles, i.e. small pointy projections resembling the spikes of a hedgehog. Investigations aimed at finding a hedgehog equivalent in vertebrates by Philip Ingham, Andrew P. McMahon and Clifford Tabin revealed three homologous genes. Two of these genes, desert hedgehog and Indian hedgehog, were named for species of hedgehogs,  while sonic hedgehog was named after the video game character Sonic the Hedgehog. The gene was named by Robert Riddle, a postdoctoral fellow at the Tabin Lab, after his wife Betsy Wilder came home with a magazine containing an advert for the first game in the series, Sonic the Hedgehog (1991). [...] acting as a morphogen involved in patterning many systems—including the anterior pituitary, pallium of the brain, spinal cord, lungs, teeth and the thalamus [...] In vertebrates, the development of limbs and digits depends on the secretion of sonic hedgehog [...] The gene has been linked to a condition known as holoprosencephaly, which can result in severe brain, skull and facial defects, causing a few clinicians and scientists to criticize the name on the grounds that it sounds too frivolous. It has been noted that mention of a mutation in a sonic hedgehog gene might not be well received in a discussion of a serious disorder with a patient or their family. [...] This controversy has largely died down [...] is largely avoided by using standardized abbreviations when speaking with patients and their families.

gancho: O esqueleto de Ricardo III, achado em 2012 sob um estacionamento, foi identificado pelo DNA de descendentes da irmã dele. Já o cromossomo Y não bateu com o da linha paterna: algum pai registrado não era o biológico.
explicacao: Ricardo III, último rei inglês morto em batalha, caiu em Bosworth em 1485 e foi enterrado numa cova tosca na igreja do convento de Greyfriars, em Leicester. O túmulo se perdeu depois que o convento foi fechado, em 1538, e surgiu até uma versão errada de que os ossos tinham sido jogados num rio. Antes da escavação, o historiador John Ashdown-Hill usou genealogia para achar descendentes de Ana de York, irmã do rei, por linha exclusivamente feminina, que herdam o mesmo DNA mitocondrial. Em 2012, nas valas abertas num estacionamento em Leicester, logo no primeiro dia apareceu o esqueleto de um homem na casa dos 30 anos, com escoliose e ferimentos graves. O DNA mitocondrial dele coincidiu com o de Michael Ibsen, descendente de Ana, e com o de outra descendente pela linha materna, numa linhagem relativamente rara. A geneticista Turi King comparou também o cromossomo Y, herdado de pai para filho, com o de quatro descendentes vivos de João de Gaunt pela linha masculina. Os quatro batiam entre si, mas não com o esqueleto, o que sugere uma falsa paternidade em algum ponto das 19 gerações entre Ricardo III e Henry Somerset, 5º duque de Beaufort. Pesquisas de King e colegas indicam que a taxa histórica de falsa paternidade fica em torno de 1% a 2% por geração.

fontes.titulo: Exhumation and reburial of Richard III of England
fontes.trecho: On 25 August 2012, in Leicester, England, the remains of Richard III, the last English king killed in battle and last king of the House of York, were discovered within the site of the former Greyfriars Friary. [...] Richard III, the final ruler of the Plantagenet dynasty, was killed on 22 August 1485 in the Battle of Bosworth Field [...] His body was taken to Greyfriars, where it was buried in a crude grave in the friary church. Following the friary's dissolution in 1538 and subsequent demolition, Richard's tomb was lost. An erroneous account arose that Richard's bones had been thrown into the River Soar at the nearby Bow Bridge. [...] On the first day, a human skeleton belonging to a man in his thirties was uncovered showing signs of severe injuries. The skeleton, which had several unusual physical features, most notably scoliosis [...] In 2005, John Ashdown-Hill announced that he had discovered the mitochondrial DNA sequence of Richard III after identifying two matrilineal descendants of Richard III's sister Anne of York. [...] It was decided to open two trenches in the Social Services car park [...] Ashdown-Hill turned instead to genealogical research to identify an all-female-line descendant of Cecily Neville, Richard's mother. [...] Analysts found a mitochondrial DNA match among the exhumed skeleton, Michael Ibsen, and a second direct maternal line descendant, who shares a relatively rare mitochondrial DNA sequence, haplogroup J1c2c. [...] Despite the matching mitochondrial DNA, geneticist Turi King continued to pursue a link between the paternally-inherited Y DNA and that of descendants of John of Gaunt. Four living male-line descendants of Gaunt have been located, and their results are a match to each other. The Y DNA from the skeleton is somewhat degraded, but proved not to match any of the living male-line relatives, suggesting that a false-paternity event had happened somewhere in the 19 generations between Richard III and Henry Somerset, 5th Duke of Beaufort; work by Turi King and others has shown that historical rates of false paternity are around 1–2% per generation.

gancho: Por décadas, Anna Anderson sustentou ser Anastasia, a filha do último czar que teria escapado do fuzilamento. Anos depois da morte dela, o DNA de um pedaço do seu intestino, guardado num hospital, desfez a história.
explicacao: Anastasia foi morta com os pais e os irmãos por revolucionários bolcheviques em Iecaterimburgo, em 17 de julho de 1918, mas o local do corpo dela ficou desconhecido até 2007. Em 1920, uma jovem sem identidade tentou se matar em Berlim e foi internada; em 1922, ganhou atenção pública a alegação de que ela era uma grã-duquesa russa. Parentes e pessoas que conheciam Anastasia a chamaram de impostora, e em 1927 uma investigação paga por um irmão da czarina a identificou como Franziska Schanzkowska, operária polonesa com histórico de doença mental. Ainda assim, muita gente acreditou nela, e uma longa disputa na justiça alemã terminou sem que ela provasse ser Anastasia. Anderson morreu em 1984 e foi cremada. Depois do fim da União Soviética, os restos da família imperial foram achados: o DNA mitocondrial das ossadas femininas bateu com o do príncipe Philip, duque de Edimburgo, cuja avó materna era irmã da czarina. Um trecho de intestino de Anderson, retirado numa cirurgia em 1979 e guardado num hospital da Virgínia, foi comparado com esse DNA: não batia com o dos Romanov, mas batia com o de Karl Maucher, neto de uma irmã de Franziska Schanzkowska. Mais tarde, em 2007, apareceram os dois últimos corpos, e testes repetidos mostraram que nenhuma das quatro filhas sobreviveu.

fontes.trecho: was an impostor who claimed to be Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia. Anastasia, the youngest daughter of the last Tsar and Tsarina of Russia, Nicholas II and Alexandra, was murdered along with her parents and siblings on 17 July 1918 by Bolshevik revolutionaries in Yekaterinburg, Russia, but the location of her body was unknown until 2007. In 1920, Anderson was institutionalized in a mental hospital after a suicide attempt in Berlin. [...] In March 1922, claims that Anderson was a Russian grand duchess received public attention. Most members of Grand Duchess Anastasia's family and those who had known her, including court tutor Pierre Gilliard, said Anderson was an impostor but others were convinced she was Anastasia. In 1927, a private investigation funded by the Tsarina's brother, Ernest Louis, Grand Duke of Hesse, identified Anderson as Franziska Schanzkowska, a Polish factory worker with a history of mental illness. After a lawsuit lasting many years, the German courts ruled that Anderson had failed to prove she was Anastasia [...] Upon her death in 1984, Anderson's body was cremated [...] After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the locations of the bodies of the Tsar, Tsarina, and all five of their children were revealed. [...] mitochondrial DNA from the female bones matched that of Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, whose maternal grandmother Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine was a sister of Alexandra. The bodies of Tsarevich Alexei and the remaining daughter were discovered in 2007. Repeated and independent DNA tests confirmed that the remains were the seven members of the Romanov family, and proved that none of the Tsar's four daughters survived the shooting of the Romanov family. A sample of Anderson's tissue, part of her intestine removed during an operation in 1979, had been stored at Martha Jefferson Hospital, Charlottesville, Virginia. [...] It did not match that of the Duke of Edinburgh or that of the bones, confirming that Anderson was not related to the Romanovs. However, the sample matched DNA provided by Karl Maucher, a grandson of Franziska Schanzkowska's sister, Gertrude (Schanzkowska) Ellerik

gancho: Nancy Wexler, filha de uma mulher com doença de Huntington, ajudou a localizar o gene da doença estudando famílias de vilarejos à beira do lago Maracaibo, na Venezuela. Em 2020, ela contou que também tem a doença.
explicacao: A doença de Huntington é hereditária e fatal. Na família da mãe de Nancy, Leonore, três irmãos dela tiveram a doença e morreram com poucos anos de diferença; o diagnóstico foi mantido em segredo, e eles eram chamados de "nervosos". Leonore tinha lido, erradamente, que a doença só atingia homens, e quando os sintomas dela começaram, o ex-marido escondeu o diagnóstico por cerca de um ano. Ela morreu em 1978. Nancy, psicóloga clínica cuja única formação formal em biologia foi um curso introdutório, fez a tese sobre como é viver sob o risco de ter a doença. Em povoados à beira do lago Maracaibo, como Barranquitas e Lagunetas, a doença era especialmente comum. A partir de 1979, a equipe dela fez ali um estudo de 20 anos: coletou mais de 4 mil amostras de sangue e documentou 18 mil pessoas para montar uma genealogia comum. As amostras foram decisivas para que um grupo internacional achasse o gene, na ponta do cromossomo 4, o que levou a um teste genético. Nancy e a irmã decidiram não ter filhos, e ela passou anos sem fazer o teste. Em 2020, numa entrevista ao New York Times, revelou que tem a doença.

fontes.trecho: The daughter of someone exhibiting Huntington's, she led a research team into a remote part of Venezuela where the disease is prevalent. [...] The samples her team collected were instrumental in allowing a global collaborative research group to locate the gene that causes the disease. [...] Leonore looked up Huntington's disease (HD) at the library and read that it was a fatal, inherited disease, and (incorrectly) that it only affecting men. Leonore's three brothers, Seymour, Paul, and Jesse Sabin, all had HD and died within four years of each other. The diagnosis was kept a secret from the rest of the family for many years. The uncles were called "nervous," instead of ill. When Leonore started showing symptoms of HD, her then ex-husband, Milton, kept the diagnosis from her for about a year. [...] She earned a Ph.D. in clinical psychology but instead chose to work in the field of genetics. [...] which constitutes "[her] only formal education in biology." [...] Wexler did her thesis on Huntington's disease, focusing on how it felt to be at risk for the disease. [...] Wexler and the team travelled to Barranquitas and Lagunetas, two settlements on Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela, where villagers had a particularly high occurrence of Huntington's. Starting in 1979, the team conducted a twenty-year-long study in which they collected over 4,000 blood samples and documented 18,000 different individuals to work out a common pedigree. The discovery that the gene was on the tip of chromosome 4 led to the development of a test for the disease. [...] She died on Mother's Day, 1978. [...] "When my sister and I both decided not to have children," she says [...] Nancy Wexler revealed in a 2020 New York Times interview that she has Huntington's disease. An episode of The Gene also tells the story of her learning she has Huntington's disease after years of not getting tested.

gancho: Em Oxford, quando o parceiro levou o arame em gancho, a corva Betty dobrou um arame reto, fez o próprio gancho e pescou um baldinho de comida num tubo. Era a primeira vez que essas aves recebiam arame.
explicacao: Betty e Abel eram dois corvos-da-nova-caledônia observados em 2002 por Alex Kacelnik e colegas, na Universidade de Oxford. O teste pedia que escolhessem entre um arame reto e um curvo para alcançar pedacinhos de coração de porco, a comida preferida deles, num baldinho dentro de um tubo vertical. O talento de Betty apareceu por acaso: quando Abel fugiu com o arame curvo, ela entortou o reto, em geral prendendo uma ponta embaixo de algo, e içou o balde. Em estudos seguintes, das dez vezes em que pegou a comida, ela dobrou o arame em nove. Na natureza, a espécie já fabrica ferramentas: cutuca larvas em frestas até que elas mordam o graveto e arranca tiras de folhas de pandano, cujas farpas servem de anzol. O arame, porém, era um material novo. Outros testes mostraram que esses corvos usam uma ferramenta para conseguir outra: com um graveto curto demais para a comida, iam buscar numa caixa um graveto mais longo. Seis de sete aves resolveram isso na primeira tentativa, algo antes só visto em primatas. Em 2016, uma equipe liderada por Christian Rutz mostrou que dobrar ferramentas faz parte do comportamento natural da espécie na natureza, e Betty tinha sido capturada na natureza ainda jovem. Isso não apaga o feito, mas sugere que ela pode ter levado ao arame um movimento que a espécie já conhecia.

fontes.trecho: In 2002, researcher Alex Kacelnik and colleagues at the University of Oxford observed of a couple of New Caledonian crows called Betty and Abel [...] Betty's toolmaking abilities came to light by accident during an experiment in which she and Abel had to choose between a hooked and a straight wire for retrieving small pieces of pig heart, their favorite food. When Abel made off with the hooked wire, Betty bent the straight wire into a hook and used the tool to lift a small bucket of food from a vertical pipe. This experiment was the first time the crows had been presented with wire. [...] Out of ten successful retrievals, Betty bent the wire into a hook nine times. [...] usually by snagging one end of the wire under something [...] The New Caledonian crow sometimes captures grubs in nooks or crevices by poking a twig at the grub to agitate it into biting the twig [...] The crows can also make leaf tools by tearing rectangular strips off the edges of Pandanus spp. [...] the barbs running along the edges of these leaves can be used as hooks [...] The crows were given a stick that was too short to reach the food.  However, this short stick could be used to retrieve a longer stick from another box, which could then be used to retrieve the food. [...] It was solved by six of seven birds on the first attempt.  This behaviour had previously only been observed in primates. In a study conducted at the Max Planck Society crows have been shown to create compound tools from 2–4 short branches that could be slotted together.

fontes.titulo: Tool bending in New Caledonian crows (Royal Society Open Science, 2016, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Author for correspondence: Christian Rutz [...] 2016 [...] Recent field experiments have revealed that tool bending is part of the species' natural behavioural repertoire, providing important context for interpreting Betty's iconic wire-bending feat. [...] Our findings therefore suggest that Betty, who had been wild-caught as a young bird, may well have expressed behaviours during test trials that were an existing part of her natural repertoire, rather than innovative solutions to an unfamiliar problem.

gancho: Pesquisadores usaram uma máscara ao capturar corvos em Seattle. Depois, corvos que nunca tinham sido pegos, até filhotes, também davam gritos de alarme contra quem usasse a máscara: o perigo passou de corvo para corvo.
explicacao: O experimento foi feito pelo laboratório de John Marzluff, professor da Universidade de Washington. Usando uma máscara de "rosto perigoso", a equipe capturou, anilhou e soltou de 7 a 15 corvos-americanos selvagens em cada um de cinco locais em volta de Seattle. Os corvos capturados passaram a repreender a máscara com gritos assim que a viam, sinal de que tinham aprendido o perigo. O surpreendente veio depois: corvos que nunca tinham sido capturados também gritavam contra ela, o que indica que aprenderam com o bando que se juntou durante as capturas. Filhotes de pais capturados também aprenderam a repreender a máscara aos gritos, ou seja, a informação passou tanto entre colegas quanto de pais para filhos. Os corvos capturados diretamente distinguiam melhor a máscara perigosa de uma máscara neutra do que os que aprenderam com os outros. Num dos locais, ao longo de cinco anos, a frequência dos gritos contra a máscara dobrou e se espalhou por pelo menos 1,2 km a partir do ponto inicial. É um exemplo de transmissão cultural: um conhecimento que circula pelo grupo sem que cada indivíduo precise passar pela experiência.

fontes.trecho: The University of Washington studied this phenomenon with crows [...] The experimenters exposed wild crows to a unique "dangerous face" mask as they trapped, banded, and released 7–15 birds at five different study places around Seattle, WA. An immediate scolding response to the mask after trapping by previously captured crows illustrates that the individual crow learned the danger of that mask. [...] That response indicates conditioning from the mob of birds that assembled during the capture. Horizontal social learning (learning from peers) is consistent with the lone crows that recognized the dangerous face without ever being captured. Children of captured crow parents were conditioned to scold the dangerous mask, which demonstrates vertical social learning (learning from parents). The crows that were captured directly had the most precise discrimination between dangerous and neutral masks than the crows that learned from the experience of their peers. The ability of crows to learn doubled the frequency of scolding, which spread at least 1.2  km from where the experiment started to over a 5-year period at one site.

John Marzluff (born 1958) is a professor of wildlife science at the University of Washington and an author. [...] His lab once banded American crows while wearing various masks, which demonstrated that crows identify and remember people's faces. After the people wearing the mask left, even crows that did not witness the tagging scolded the mask, showing an example of cultural transmission in crows.

gancho: A abelha que acha flores dança no favo: o ângulo da dança em relação ao "para cima" copia o ângulo da flor em relação ao Sol. Mas, num experimento, 93% das veteranas que seguiram a dança foram a lugares já conhecidos.
explicacao: O austríaco Karl von Frisch foi um dos primeiros a decifrar a chamada dança do requebrado. A abelha percorre um oito: faz uma corrida reta requebrando, contorna de volta ao ponto de partida e repete. Nos favos verticais, dentro do ninho escuro, a corrida apontada para cima representa a direção do Sol, e um ângulo à direita ou à esquerda da vertical indica o mesmo ângulo em relação ao Sol. A distância vai na duração do requebrado: segundo von Frisch, cerca de um segundo para cada quilômetro. Abelhas que passam muito tempo dançando corrigem o ângulo conforme o Sol se move no céu. Von Frisch também concluiu que, sob nuvens, elas podem se guiar pelo padrão de luz polarizada do céu azul, invisível para nós. A teoria, descrita num livro de 1927, enfrentou ceticismo e só décadas depois foi reconhecida; em 1973, von Frisch dividiu o Nobel de Fisiologia ou Medicina com Konrad Lorenz e Nikolaas Tinbergen. O quanto as abelhas usam essa informação, porém, segue em debate. Num experimento com a abelha-europeia, a maioria das campeiras experientes, que já conheciam uma fonte de comida, ignorou direção e distância mesmo depois de acompanhar a dança com atenção, e 93% voltaram a áreas que já conheciam. As abelhas também acham comida pelo cheiro e pela memória, e a dança pesa mais quando o alimento é escasso.

fontes.trecho: Austrian ethologist and Nobel laureate Karl von Frisch was one of the first who translated the meaning of the waggle dance. [...] A worker bee's waggle dance involves running through a small figure-eight pattern: a waggle run (aka waggle phase) followed by a turn to the right to circle back to the starting point [...] flowers that are located directly in line with the sun are represented by waggle runs in an upward direction on the vertical combs, and any angle to the right or left of the sun is coded by a corresponding angle to the right or left of the upward direction. The distance between hive and recruitment target is encoded in the duration of the waggle runs. [...] Waggle dancing bees that have been in the nest for an extended time adjust the angles of their dances to accommodate the changing direction of the sun. [...] Honeybees are able to successfully forage independently using olfactory cues and by remembering the location of previously rewarding food sites. [...] the waggle dance plays a significantly larger role in foraging when food sources are not as abundant. [...] the cavity-nesting bees are able to use gravity and orient their dances in their dark nests. [...] In an experiment on the honeybee Apis mellifera, most individuals who thoroughly followed a waggle dance ignored the resource direction and location information. Instead, 93% of the foragers returned to foraging areas they had previous knowledge of.

Karl Ritter von Frisch (20 November 1886 – 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz. [...] His theory, described in his 1927 book [...] was disputed by other scientists and met with widespread skepticism at the time, only decades later being appreciated as both zoologically accurate [...] He discovered that bees can recognize the desired compass direction in three different ways: by the Sun, by the polarization pattern of the blue sky, and by the Earth's magnetic field, whereby the Sun is used as the main compass, with the alternatives reserved for the conditions arising under cloudy skies or within a dark beehive. Light scattered in a blue sky forms a characteristic pattern of partially polarized light which is dependent on the position of the Sun and invisible to human eyes. [...] The distance to the food source is relayed by the time taken to traverse the straight stretch, one second indicating a distance of approximately one kilometer

gancho: Um enxame de abelhas sem casa escolhe o novo lar quase por votação: centenas de batedoras visitam ocos e fazem campanha dançando, e o enxame só parte quando um local reúne um quórum de apoiadoras.
explicacao: O enxame é o jeito de uma colônia de abelhas se reproduzir: ela se divide em duas ou mais. Antes, as operárias param de alimentar a rainha, porque uma rainha em postura fica pesada demais para voos longos. Ao sair, o enxame não vai longe: pousa num galho a poucos metros e se aglomera em volta da rainha, enquanto algumas centenas de batedoras procuram ocos adequados. Cada batedora que volta anuncia o local achado com a dança do requebrado, que indica direção, distância e qualidade, e quanto mais animada ela está, mais animada é a dança. Se convence outras, elas vão conferir e, se aprovarem, também passam a promover o local. No começo, vários candidatos disputam apoio; depois de horas, às vezes dias, um favorito vai emergindo. Há pressa: o enxame só aguenta cerca de três dias com o mel que levou no estômago. A decisão costuma sair quando há um quórum de cerca de 15 a 30 batedoras num mesmo local. Então o enxame inteiro decola e pode voar um quilômetro ou mais, guiado por batedoras que passam rápido por cima do grupo na direção certa. Esse processo coletivo costuma acertar o melhor local e manter o enxame unido.

fontes.trecho: Swarming is a honey bee colony's natural means of reproduction. In the process of swarming, a single colony splits into two or more distinct colonies. [...] A laying queen is too heavy to fly long distances. Therefore, the workers will stop feeding her before the anticipated swarm date and the queen will stop laying eggs. [...] When a honey bee swarm emerges from a hive they do not fly far at first. They may gather in a tree or on a branch only a few metres (yards) from the hive. There they cluster about the queen [...] An individual scout returning to the cluster promotes a location she has found. She uses the waggle dance to indicate its direction, distance, and quality to others in the cluster. The more excited she is about her findings, the more excitedly she dances. If she can convince other scouts to check out the location she found, they take off, check out the proposed site, and choose to promote the site further upon their return. Several sites may be promoted by different scouts at first. After several hours and sometimes days, a favorite location gradually emerges from this decision-making process. In order for a decision to be made in a relatively short amount of time (the swarm can only survive for about three days on the honey on which they gorged themselves before leaving the hive), a decision will often be made when somewhere around 80% of the scouts have agreed upon a single location and/or when there is a quorum of 20–30 scouts present at a potential nest site. [...] When the scout bees agree where to nest, the whole clustered swarm takes off and flies to it. A swarm may fly a kilometer or more to the scouted location, with the scouts guiding the rest of the bees by quickly flying overhead in the proper direction. This collective decision-making process is remarkably successful in identifying the most suitable new nest site and keeping the swarm intact.

fontes.titulo: How 10,000 bees decide where to go when they fly the coop (Cornell Chronicle, 2006)
fontes.trecho: Their technique, says Cornell University biologist Thomas Seeley, includes coalition building until a quorum develops. [...] As soon as 15 or more bees are at any one site, the researchers found, the scouts signal to the waiting bees in the swarm that it's time to warm up their flight muscles in preparation for takeoff. [...] When a hive gets too crowded, its queen and half the hive will swarm to a nearby tree and quietly wait while several hundred scouts go house hunting.

gancho: No zoológico sueco de Furuvik, o chimpanzé Santino juntava pedras de manhã, calmo, antes de o público chegar, para atirá-las nos visitantes horas depois. Mais tarde, passou a esconder seus projéteis sob montes de feno.
explicacao: Santino nasceu em 1978 no zoológico de Munique e foi levado aos cinco anos para Furuvik, na Suécia. Em 1997, começou a recolher pedras do fosso em volta da ilha onde vivia e a guardá-las horas antes de atirá-las nos visitantes que chegavam, em exibições de dominância. Ao limpar a ilha, os tratadores acharam montes de pedras na margem voltada para o público, e uma tratadora escondida o viu empilhá-las pela manhã. A partir de 1998, ele também arrancava pedaços soltos do concreto para usar como projéteis. Chamou a atenção que ficasse calmo ao juntar as pedras e agitado só na hora dos arremessos, sinal de preparação para algo futuro. Em 2010, o pesquisador Mathias Osvath, da Universidade de Lund, e Elin Karvonen registraram uma novidade: Santino passou a cobrir projéteis com feno e a deixá-los atrás de troncos, perto dos visitantes, e se aproximava sem a exibição agressiva de costume antes de atirar. Dos 46 projéteis recolhidos no período, muitos deles pedaços de concreto, 35 estavam escondidos. Críticos do primeiro relato, de 2009, lembraram que ninguém registrou como surgiram os primeiros montes de pedras, o que deixa aberta a interpretação. Para conter o comportamento, os tratadores castraram Santino. Ele morreu em 2022, baleado após fugir do recinto.

fontes.titulo: Spontaneous innovation for future deception in a male chimpanzee (PLoS ONE, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: The male chimpanzee, Santino, was born in 1978 at Munich Zoo in West Germany. At the age of five, he was transferred to Furuvik Zoo, Sweden [...] In 1997 the chimpanzee started to gather stones from the water moat surrounding the outside compound and storing them hours before he threw them in dominance displays at the arriving zoo visitors. [...] When cleaning the island compound, the zookeepers found five stone caches placed at the shoreline facing the visitors' area. Following days a zookeeper placed herself in a blind to observe the chimpanzee behaviour during the morning hours. He was found to retrieve stones from the moat and place them in piles. In 1998, the chimpanzee started to manufacture projectiles by breaking off loose pieces from the compound's concrete surface [...] calm during the gathering process, agitated during the throwing sessions [...] he typically collected projectiles in the morning before the zoo opened [...] manufactured concealments from hay, as well as used naturally occurring concealments. All were placed near the visitors' observation area [...] hiding projectiles and inhibiting dominance display behaviour [...] This study was carried out in 2010 [...] In all, 46 projectiles were recovered, of which 35 came from concealments. [...] 18 were placed behind logs [...] concerns have been raised over how the findings should be interpreted – because no detailed data is available on the chimpanzee's behaviour and circumstances at the moment when the first caches were made [...] In 2009 one of us (MO) reported on the projectile related behaviour of the male chimpanzee [...] The projectiles were chipped off the surface layer of the concrete in the outdoor compound island immediately before they were used. [...] with two concrete projectiles in his hand [...] recovered twelve remaining projectiles from the island, all from concrete

Santino (20 April 1978 – 14 December 2022) was a male chimpanzee held at Furuvik Zoo in Sweden. [...] Dr. Mathias Osvath, a cognitive zoologist from Lund University, together with Elin Karvonen, studied the phenomenon [...] To control his behaviour, and keep his hormone levels down, zookeepers castrated Santino. [...] Santino was shot after escaping his enclosure in December 2022, and later died from his injuries.

gancho: Um polvo da Indonésia recolhe metades de casca de coco jogadas fora por humanos, carrega-as por até 20 metros e depois as monta em volta do corpo como um abrigo portátil.
explicacao: O polvo-do-coco (Amphioctopus marginatus) vive em águas tropicais do Pacífico ocidental e do Índico e prefere fundos de areia com muitas conchas ou lixo. Em 2009, pesquisadores do Museu de Melbourne, na Austrália, descreveram polvos dessa espécie, filmados em Bali e no norte de Sulawesi, recolhendo do fundo do mar metades de casca de coco descartadas por pessoas. Eles levavam as cascas por até 20 metros e depois as montavam em volta do corpo, formando um esconderijo esférico parecido com uma concha de molusco. Outros polvos já tinham sido vistos usando conchas para se esconder. A novidade foi juntar e transportar o material para usar mais tarde, o que o museu chamou de "uso verdadeiro de ferramenta". Nem todos concordam: para outros biólogos, a casca é só uma proteção contínua contra predadores, e não uma ferramenta. A espécie também se abriga em conchas de moluscos e até em garrafas. E tem outra esquisitice: é uma das duas únicas espécies de polvo conhecidas que andam sobre dois braços. Enquanto "caminha" com dois, usa os outros seis para se disfarçar, e os pesquisadores especularam que o disfarce imitaria um coco rolando.

fontes.trecho: Amphioctopus marginatus, also known as the coconut octopus and veined octopus, is a medium-sized cephalopod found in the tropical waters of the western Pacific Ocean and the Indian Ocean. It prefers sandy substrates with plentiful shells or litter. It commonly preys upon shrimp, crabs, and clams, and displays unusual behavior for octopuses, being one of only two species known to exhibit bipedal walking. [...] This involves rolling two arms to walk while the other six arms are used to disguise itself; the researchers speculated that the disguise might be meant to mimic the appearance of a rolling coconut. [...] In 2009, researchers from the Melbourne Museum in Australia observed the coconut octopus using tools for concealment and defense by gathering available debris to create a shelter. The researchers filmed the octopus collecting coconut half-shells from the sea floor that had been discarded by humans. They were then carried up to 20 meters (66 ft) and arranged around the body of the octopus to form a spherical hiding place similar to a clamshell. This behavior was observed in specimen in Bali and North Sulawesi, Indonesia, and is likely the first evidence of tool use in invertebrates. Other species of octopus had been observed using shells for hiding, but this was the first case in which shells were prepared and collected for later use, in what the Melbourne Museum has described as "true tool use". [...] The coconut octopus has been observed using a variety of materials for shelter, including coconut shells, clamshells, and man-made litter such as bottles.

The authors of the research article claimed this behaviour falls under the definition of tool use because the shells are carried for later use. However, this argument remains contested by a number of other biologists who state that the shells actually provide continuous protection from abundant bottom-dwelling predators in their home range.

gancho: O pássaro-lira imita motosserras e obturadores de câmera, mas bem menos do que a fama sugere: no famoso trecho de Attenborough que mostra essas imitações, duas das três aves filmadas viviam em cativeiro.
explicacao: Os pássaros-lira da Austrália são mestres da imitação: copiam com fidelidade o canto de outras aves, o burburinho de bandos inteiros e até sons de possuns (marsupiais australianos), coalas e dingos. Já foram gravados reproduzindo serrote, motosserra, motor e alarme de carro, tiro, obturador de câmera, latido, choro de bebê, toque de celular e voz humana. Mas a imitação de ruídos humanos, embora muito divulgada, é exagerada. No episódio da série "The Life of Birds", de David Attenborough, um macho aparece imitando alarme de carro, motosserra e obturadores, só que duas das três aves mostradas eram de cativeiro. Partes do canto natural do pássaro-lira lembram efeitos sonoros, o que alimentou a lenda urbana de que eles imitam com frequência sons de videogames e filmes. As imitações humanas existem: a gravação de um pássaro-lira imitando um jogo eletrônico de tiro, operários e motosserras entrou em 2013 no registro Sounds of Australia, do arquivo nacional de som e imagem do país. Já a história de um pássaro-lira de estimação que, nos anos 1930, teria aprendido melodias de um flautista e as levado para a mata nunca foi comprovada: um grupo de pesquisa não conseguiu provar que a ave tinha sido de estimação, embora tenha reconhecido indícios dos dois lados.

fontes.trecho: Lyrebirds render with great fidelity the individual songs of other birds and the chatter of flocks of birds, and also mimic other animals, such as possums, koalas, and dingoes. Lyrebirds have been recorded mimicking human sounds such as a mill whistle, a cross-cut saw, chainsaws, car engines and car alarms, fire alarms, rifle-shots, camera shutters, dogs barking, crying babies, music, mobile-phone ring tones, and even the human voice. While the mimicry of human noises is widely reported, the extent to which it happens is exaggerated. Parts of the lyrebird's own song can resemble human-made sound effects, which has given rise to the urban legend that they frequently imitate video game or film sounds. [...] A recording of a superb lyrebird mimicking sounds of an electronic shooting game, workmen, and chainsaws was added to the National Film and Sound Archive's Sounds of Australia registry in 2013. [...] in the 1930s, a flute player living on a farm adjoining the park used to play tunes near his pet lyrebird. [...] However, a "flute lyrebird" research group (including Curtis and Fenton) formed to investigate the veracity of this story [...] Neither was able to prove that a lyrebird chick had been a pet [...] although they acknowledged compelling evidence on both sides of the argument

In David Attenborough's Life of Birds (ep. 6), the superb lyrebird is described as able to imitate twenty bird species' calls, and a male is shown mimicking a car alarm, chainsaw, and various camera shutters. However, two of the three lyrebirds featured were captive birds.

gancho: Uma ave africana, o drongo, avisa outros bichos quando há predador. Mas às vezes dá alarme falso, até imitando o alarme deles, para que larguem a comida e ele a roube. E muda o grito quando a vítima para de acreditar.
explicacao: O drongo-de-cauda-forcada (Dicrurus adsimilis) passa cerca de 29% do tempo seguindo outros animais que procuram comida no chão, como suricatos e uma ave chamada Turdoides bicolor. Ele costuma dar alarmes verdadeiros quando um predador aparece. Mas, quando vê um desses animais segurando comida, pode soltar um alarme falso: o alvo corre para se abrigar, larga o alimento e o drongo o pega. Um estudo de campo mostrou que os alarmes falsos podem ser do repertório do próprio drongo ou imitações do alarme de outras espécies, e que não diferem na estrutura dos alarmes verdadeiros. Em experimentos com gravações, suricatos e Turdoides caíram nos dois tipos. O problema de mentir é que a vítima aprende. Um estudo posterior confirmou que as espécies-alvo passam a reagir menos a um alarme falso repetido, mas mantêm o medo quando o chamado muda. E os drongos exploram justamente isso: trocam de tipo de alarme quando tentam roubar várias vezes da mesma espécie, driblando o limite que costuma tornar a mentira pouco vantajosa.

fontes.titulo: Fork-tailed drongos use deceptive mimicked alarm calls to steal food (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2011, resumo via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Here, I show that wild fork-tailed drongos (Dicrurus adsimilis) make both drongo-specific and mimicked false alarm calls when watching target species handling food, in response to which targets flee to cover abandoning their food. The drongo-specific and mimicked calls made in false alarms were structurally indistinguishable from calls made during true alarms at predators by drongos and other species. Furthermore, I demonstrate by playback experiments that two of these species, meerkats (Suricata suricatta) and pied babblers (Turdoides bicolor), are deceived by both drongo-specific and mimicked false alarm calls.

fontes.titulo: Deception by flexible alarm mimicry in an African bird (Science, 2014, resumo via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Deception is common in nature, but victims of deception discriminate against and ultimately ignore deceptive signals when they are produced too frequently. [...] Fork-tailed drongos (Dicrurus adsimilis) use false alarm calls to scare other species away from food that they then steal. We show that drongos mimic the alarms of targeted species. Further, target species reduce their response to false alarm calls when they are repeated. However, the fear response is maintained when the call is varied. Drongos exploit this propensity by changing their alarm-call type when making repeated theft attempts on a particular species. Our results show that drongos can evade the frequency-dependent constraints that typically limit deception payoffs through flexible variation of their alarm calls.

The drongo will give genuine alarm calls to signal the presence of predators to other animals, but occasionally, it will issue a false alarm call to displace those animals and steal their food. [...] It has been observed that fork-tailed drongos spend approximately 29% of their time trailing other animals. Species such as southern pied babblers, sociable weavers, wattled starlings and meerkats, which forage on the ground, are often targeted

gancho: O "efeito do centésimo macaco", em que um hábito saltaria por si só a ilhas vizinhas ao atingir massa crítica, é lenda. Os macacos japoneses que lavavam batata aprenderam devagar, e a colônia inteira tinha só 59 em 1962.
explicacao: A história real começou na ilha japonesa de Koshima, onde, em 1952 e 1953, primatólogos deixavam batata-doce e trigo na praia para estudar um bando de macacos-japoneses. Em 1954, um artigo relatou que uma macaca, Imo, lavava as batatas na água. O hábito se espalhou aos poucos, primeiro entre os jovens e suas famílias, por observação e imitação; os mais velhos em geral não aprendiam, e a fração de lavadores cresceu à medida que eles morriam e nasciam filhotes. Imo inventou ainda um jeito de separar trigo da areia: jogava punhados na água e pegava os grãos que boiavam. Nos anos 1970, o escritor Lyall Watson transformou o caso numa parábola: ao chegar a um número crítico, o hábito teria passado de repente a macacos de ilhas vizinhas. Ken Keyes popularizou a versão num livro de 1984, e ela virou lenda da Nova Era. Em 1985, uma revisão dos relatórios originais concluiu que eles não sustentavam a história. Além disso, os bandos das várias ilhas tinham os pesquisadores em comum, e a colônia de Koshima somava 59 macacos em 1962: não havia nem um centésimo macaco. O estudo original continua útil para entender a transmissão cultural entre animais.

fontes.trecho: The hundredth monkey effect is an esoteric idea claiming that a new behavior or idea is spread rapidly by unexplained means from one group to all related groups once a critical number of members of one group exhibit the new behavior or acknowledge the new idea. [...] The "hundredth monkey" effect was popularized in the mid-to-late 1970s by Lyall Watson [...] Between 1952 and 1953, primatologists conducted a behavioral study of a troop of Macaca fuscata (Japanese macaque or snow monkeys) on the island of Kōjima. The researchers would supply these troops with such foods as sweet potatoes and wheat in open areas, often on beaches. [...] In 1954, a paper was published indicating the first observances of one monkey, Imo, washing her sweet potatoes in the water. [...] The young first teach their contemporaries and immediate family [...] The young monkey who started potato washing also learned how to sift wheat grains out of the sand by throwing handfuls of sand and wheat into the water, then catching the wheat that floated to the top. [...] This story was further popularized by Ken Keyes Jr. with the publication of his book The Hundredth Monkey (1984). [...] In 1985, Elaine Myers re-examined the original published research [...] she found that the original research reports by the Japan Monkey Centre in the 2nd, 5th, and 6th volumes of Primates were insufficient to support Watson's story. [...] The story as told by Watson and Keyes is popular among New Age authors and personal-growth gurus, as well as becoming an urban legend and part of New Age mythology. [...] The original research continues to prove useful in the study of cultural transmission in animals. [...] Claims that the practice spread suddenly to other isolated populations of monkeys may be called into question given the fact that the monkeys had the researchers in common. [...] Moreover, the number of monkeys in the colony was counted as 59 in 1962, indicating that even in numbers no "hundredth monkey" existed. [...] older monkeys who did not know how to wash tended not to learn. As the older monkeys died and younger monkeys were born the proportion of washers naturally increased.

gancho: Na África, uma ave guia caçadores de mel até colmeias silvestres e depois come a cera que sobra. Em Moçambique, ela responde a um chamado tradicional dos caçadores, um "brrrr-hmm".
explicacao: O indicador-grande (Indicator indicator), parente dos pica-paus, deve o nome ao hábito de guiar pessoas até ninhos de abelhas. Ele chama a atenção com notas trêmulas e tagarelas, voa na direção de uma colmeia ocupada (conhece a localização de muitas no seu território) e para perto dela. Os caçadores abrem a colmeia com fogo, fumaça e machados, e a ave come a cera que fica. A parceria rende aos humanos. Entre os boranas, do leste da África, a ajuda corta em cerca de dois terços o tempo de busca, e um assobio próprio para chamar a ave, o fuulido, dobra a chance de encontrá-la. No norte da Tanzânia, os indicadores aumentaram em 560% a taxa com que os hadzas achavam colmeias. No norte de Moçambique, um estudo com os caçadores yao mostrou que as aves respondem ao chamado tradicional "brrrr-hmm", que aumenta muito a chance de achar uma colmeia. Nem todos retribuem: os hadzas costumam queimar, enterrar ou esconder a cera, para manter a ave com fome e disposta a guiar de novo. E a ideia, repetida em muitas fontes, de que ela também guia o texugo-do-mel é contestada: os relatos em primeira mão são todos de guiadas incompletas.

fontes.trecho: The greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator) is a bird in the paleotropical family Indicatoridae, that is related to the woodpeckers. Its English and scientific names refer to its habit of guiding people to bee colonies. Claims that it also guides non-human animals are disputed. [...] A guiding bird attracts a person's attention with wavering, chattering "'tya' notes compounded with peeps or pipes", sounds it also gives in aggression. The guiding bird flies toward an occupied nest (greater honeyguides know the sites of many bees' nests in their territories) and then stops nearby the nest. Honey-hunters then do a final search for the bee colony, and if deemed suitable, harvest honey from the bee colony through the use of fire and smoke to subdue the bees, and axes and machetes to expose the colony. After harvesting the honey, the honeyguide eats wax that is left. One study found that use of honeyguides by the Boran people of East Africa reduces their search time for honey by approximately two-thirds. [...] The fuulido doubles the encounter rate with honeyguides. In northern Tanzania, Honeyguides increased the Hadza's rate of finding bee nests by 560% [...] Another study of the Yao honey-hunters in northern Mozambique showed that the honeyguides responded to the traditional brrrr-hmm call of the honey-hunters. The chances of finding a bee-hive were greatly increased when the traditional call was used. [...] The Hadza people of northern Tanzania frequently burn, bury, or hide the wax that lays with the intent of keeping the bird hungry, and more likely to guide again. [...] Many sources say that this species also guides honey badgers. [...] the first-hand accounts given in his review in support of this association are all of incomplete guiding sequences.

gancho: Entre 1974 e 1978, Jane Goodall acompanhou uma "guerra" entre chimpanzés na Tanzânia: um grupo que se separou do bando original foi atacado até perder todos os machos. Nem todos os cientistas acreditaram nela.
explicacao: A comunidade Kasakela, estudada por Goodall em Gombe, foi se dividindo até que seis machos adultos, três fêmeas e seus filhotes passaram a viver no sul e formaram a comunidade Kahama. Em 7 de janeiro de 1974, seis machos Kasakela emboscaram Godi, um macho Kahama que comia sozinho numa árvore, e o espancaram até ele parar de se mexer; ele provavelmente morreu pouco depois. Foi a primeira vez que se viu machos de chimpanzé tentarem deliberadamente matar outro macho. Vieram outros ataques, e em quatro anos todos os machos Kahama foram mortos ou desapareceram. O antropólogo Brian Ferguson pondera que alguns desaparecidos podem ter fugido para outra comunidade, e outros estudos lembram que um leopardo que rondava Gombe na época pode ter levado parte deles. Os vencedores tomaram o território, mas logo perderam boa parte dele para comunidades vizinhas mais numerosas. Goodall, que via os chimpanzés como "mais bonzinhos" que os humanos, ficou chocada. O relato não foi aceito por todos: houve quem a acusasse de antropomorfismo e quem dissesse que a presença dela, e o hábito de alimentar os animais, tinham criado o conflito. Pesquisas posteriores, com métodos menos invasivos, confirmaram que chimpanzés na natureza fazem guerra. Um estudo de 2018 atribuiu o conflito a uma disputa de poder entre três machos de alto escalão, agravada pela falta de fêmeas férteis.

fontes.trecho: The Gombe Chimpanzee War, also known as the Four-Year War, was a violent conflict between two communities of chimpanzees in Gombe Stream National Park in the Kigoma region of Tanzania between 1974 and 1978. The two groups were once unified in the Kasakela community. [...] a large party of chimpanzees separated themselves into the southern area of Kasakela and were renamed the Kahama community. The separatists consisted of six adult males, three adult females and their young. [...] During the four-year conflict, all males of the Kahama community were killed, effectively disbanding the community. The victorious Kasakela then expanded into further territory but were later repelled by two other communities of chimpanzees. [...] First blood was drawn by the Kasakela community on 7 January 1974, when a party of six adult Kasakela males consisting of Humphrey, Figan, Jomeo, Sherry, Evered, and Rodolf ambushed the isolated Kahama male Godi while he was feeding on a tree. [...] the attackers seized him, threw him on the ground and beat him until he stopped moving. [...] but probably died of his injuries soon after. This was the first time male chimpanzees had been seen to deliberately attempt to kill a fellow male chimpanzee. [...] After Charlie's death, Willy Wally disappeared and was never found. [...] Cowed by the superior strength and numbers of the Kalande [...] The outbreak of the war shocked her, as she had previously considered chimpanzees to be, although similar to human beings, "rather 'nicer'". [...] When Goodall reported on the events of the Gombe War, her account of a naturally occurring war between chimpanzees was not universally believed. [...] Some scientists accused her of excessive anthropomorphism; others suggested that her presence, and her practice of feeding the chimpanzees, had created violent conflict in a naturally peaceful society. However, later research using less intrusive methods confirmed that chimpanzee societies, in their natural state, indeed wage war. A 2018 study published in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology concluded that the Gombe War was most likely a consequence of a power struggle between three high-ranking males, which was exacerbated by an unusual scarcity of fertile females. [...] Ferguson argued that at least some of the missing Kahama may have survived the war by escaping the Gombe area, as the Kahama community had friendly contacts with an unstudied chimpanzee community [...] anthropologist R. Brian Ferguson [...] the Kasakela quickly gave up much of their new territory. [...] some research has suggested that the casualties of the war may have been smaller than initially reported, as a leopard had been active in Gombe at the time of the war and might have taken some of the missing chimpanzees.

gancho: Pombos treinados aprenderam a distinguir quadros de Picasso e de Monet e acertaram até telas que nunca tinham visto. Com os Monet de cabeça para baixo, porém, eles se confundiam; com os cubistas invertidos, não.
explicacao: Em 1995, Watanabe, Sakamoto e Wakita publicaram o experimento. O treino era simples: diante de um quadro de Picasso, o pombo que bicava ganhava comida; diante de um Monet, bicar era inútil. Depois de praticar com um punhado de telas, as aves passaram a bicar só os Picasso. O teste de verdade veio com quadros novos: os pombos continuaram acertando o autor e conseguiram até separar pinturas cubistas, a escola de Picasso, de impressionistas, a de Monet. Virar as telas de ponta-cabeça atrapalhou a classificação dos Monet, mas não a das obras cubistas. Num trabalho posterior, Watanabe deu o mesmo treino a pombos e a universitários para distinguir Van Gogh de Chagall, e o desempenho dos dois grupos foi parecido. O estudo rendeu aos autores o Ig Nobel de Psicologia de 1995, paródia do Nobel que premia pesquisas que "primeiro fazem rir e depois fazem pensar".

fontes.trecho: In an article from 1995, Watanabe, Sakamoto, and Wakita described an experiment which showed that pigeons can be trained to discriminate between paintings by Picasso and by Monet. The birds were first trained on a limited set of paintings. The experiment has shown that a pigeon was able to obtain food by repeated pecking when shown a painting from Picasso; when it was a Monet, pecking had no effect. After a while, the pigeons would only peck when shown Picasso paintings. They were then able to generalize and correctly discriminate between paintings of the two painters not previously shown, and even between cubist and impressionist paintings (cubism and impressionism being the two stylistic schools Picasso and Monet belong to). When the Monet paintings were shown upside down, the pigeons were not able to properly categorize anymore. Showing the cubist works upside down did not have such an effect. In 1995, the authors won the Ig Nobel Prize in psychology for this work. [...] In a later paper, Watanabe showed that if pigeons and human college students undergo the same training, their performance in distinguishing between Van Gogh and Chagall paintings is comparable.

fontes.titulo: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
